title: Ten More Minutes
excerpt: Workplace Romance · Forbidden Attraction · Slow Burn · Mature Romance
content:
Naomi regretted saying it the moment Devraj smiled.

Not because the smile was particularly wide or arrogant. It wasn't. It was the kind of smile that suggested he had discovered something interesting and intended to be patient enough to find out exactly what it was.

Ten minutes.

She had given him ten minutes, as though time were a reasonable substitute for judgment.

"You're still here," she said, snapping her cash drawer shut.

"Excellent observation."

"Don't start."

"Wouldn't dream of it."

He pushed away from the counter and reached for his jacket, which hung over the back of a chair near the service station. He moved without hurry, buttoning one cuff, then the other.

Naomi hated that she noticed his hands.

She hated even more that she had started noticing them weeks ago.

"Are you always this difficult?" she asked.

"Only when someone gives me a deadline and expects me to ignore it."

"I expect you to go home."

"I will."

"Now?"

"When you're ready."

She stared at him.

He lifted both hands. "I'm not keeping you here, Naomi. I'm offering to walk you home. If you'd rather walk alone, say so."

The answer was so reasonable that it robbed her of the argument she had prepared.

Outside, rain tapped against the restaurant windows. The city beyond the glass had settled into that peculiar stillness that belonged to the hours after midnight, when the buses were less frequent and the pavements seemed to belong to people with nowhere urgent to be.

Naomi collected her bag.

"Fine," she said. "You can walk me to the station."

"The station it is."

"And we're not discussing work."

"Agreed."

"Or the fact that you keep looking at me."

"That may be difficult."

She gave him a warning look.

"Sorry," he said, although he looked nothing of the sort.

They stepped outside together.

The cold air cleared some of the heat from Naomi's face. She tucked her hands into her coat pockets and started down the pavement, expecting Devraj to fall into step beside her.

He did.

For several minutes, they talked about harmless things. The restaurant's broken dishwasher. A customer who had sent back three perfectly good bottles of wine. The noodle shop downstairs, which Devraj insisted made the best broth in the city.

Then the conversation drifted into something more dangerous.

"Why the rule?" he asked.

Naomi kept walking.

"I told you. I don't date coworkers."

"That tells me what the rule says. It doesn't tell me why you wrote it."

She stopped beneath the awning of a closed pharmacy.

For a moment, the rain was the only sound between them.

"My last relationship ended badly," she said. "We worked together. At first, it was exciting. Secret smiles, late shifts, all that nonsense. Then we started fighting, and suddenly everybody had an opinion. People picked sides. He told our manager things about me that weren't true."

Devraj's expression changed.

"Did you lose your job?"

"No. But I nearly lost the kitchen I'd spent years trying to build."

She looked back toward the restaurant, though it was several streets away.

"I decided I would never let someone else's feelings interfere with my work again."

"That's fair."

She blinked. "That's it?"

"What were you expecting?"

"A lecture about how not everyone is the same."

"I don't know your ex. I have no intention of defending him."

Something in her chest loosened, unexpectedly.

Devraj glanced toward the crossing. "But I will say one thing."

"Of course you will."

"You don't have to decide what I am before you know me."

Naomi studied him.

"And what exactly are you asking me to know?"

He stepped a little closer, leaving enough room for her to move away.

"That I like you. That I have for a while. And that I can respect a no."

The simplicity of it unsettled her more than any practiced line could have.

She had spent two years protecting herself from men who mistook persistence for entitlement. Devraj wasn't demanding anything. He was standing in the rain, giving her a choice.

"You're making this very difficult," she whispered.

"Making what difficult?"

"Keeping my life uncomplicated."

His gaze dropped briefly to her mouth, then returned to her eyes.

"Then I won't complicate it tonight."

He took a step back.

The sudden distance between them felt larger than it should have.

They reached the station a few minutes later. Naomi turned toward him beneath the bright entrance lights.

"Goodnight, Devraj."

"Goodnight, Chef."

He started to leave.

"Devraj?"

He looked back.

She could have told him to wait. She could have asked him to kiss her. She could have done a hundred reckless things that would have made the evening impossible to forget.

Instead, she said, "You forgot your jacket."

He glanced down at the jacket draped over his arm.

"Did I?"

Naomi laughed before she could stop herself.

It was a real laugh, unguarded and bright, and Devraj looked at her as if she had just handed him something precious.

"See you tomorrow," he said.

Then he walked away.

Naomi stood at the station entrance until the rain swallowed his silhouette.

On the train home, she opened her notes app and typed a message she had no intention of sending.

I think about kissing you more than I should.

She stared at it for a long time.

Then she deleted it.

But the next morning, when she arrived at the restaurant and found a small cup of coffee waiting beside her station, she knew exactly who had left it there.

A folded napkin lay beneath the cup.

On it, in neat handwriting, were five words.

No pressure. Just good coffee.

Naomi looked toward the service entrance.

Devraj was already there, speaking with the manager, completely occupied with his work.

She picked up the coffee.

For the first time in two years, the rule above her pass looked less like protection and more like a challenge.

And she wasn't sure she wanted to win.
